valuation-methodologies-1: Because the market price is an opinion, not a fact. You value a company to see whether that opinion is wrong and what it would be worth under your own assumptions or to a specific buyer.
valuation-methodologies-2: Comps are market-based and fast but depend on finding true peers; precedents capture what buyers actually pay including control premiums but are dated and disclosure-poor; the DCF is intrinsic and assumption-driven, so it is the most theoretically sound and the easiest to manipulate.
valuation-methodologies-3: It depends, but precedent transactions usually run highest because of the control premium, and the DCF is often highest of all since you control the assumptions.
valuation-methodologies-4: The healthcare company, assuming equal growth and margins, because it is less asset-intensive — lower CapEx and working capital means more of that EBITDA becomes cash flow.
valuation-methodologies-5: Screen for peers by industry, size, and geography, calculate the metrics and multiples for each, take the median or the 25th-to-75th percentile range, and apply that range to your company's own metrics to get an implied value range.
valuation-methodologies-6: Screen on industry, size, and geography, plus a date range for transactions — for example, US steel manufacturers above $500M of revenue, or European airline deals in the past three years.
valuation-methodologies-7: Use one revenue-based multiple and one or two profitability multiples — typically TEV/Revenue, TEV/EBITDA, and P/E — so a company that screens cheap on one is tested against the others.
valuation-methodologies-8: Historical numbers actually happened but can be distorted by non-recurring items and acquisitions; projections reflect expectations but are estimates. Multiples on both tell you whether the market is paying for the past or the future.
valuation-methodologies-9: Always use current Equity Value and current Enterprise Value — never project them. The share price already reflects future expectations, so projecting it double-counts growth.
valuation-methodologies-10: If your company trades below the median with similar growth and margins, it may be undervalued; if its growth and margins are weaker, the discount is deserved. Comps only mean something when the fundamentals line up and the multiples do not.
valuation-methodologies-11: Sum the market values of all assets and subtract all liabilities. It is a floor value, useful in distress and bankruptcy, and close to meaningless for a healthy company whose value is in future cash flow.
valuation-methodologies-12: A DDM discounts dividends at the Cost of Equity to get Equity Value directly, rather than discounting free cash flow at WACC. It is used for banks and insurers, where debt is part of operations and free cash flow is not meaningful.
valuation-methodologies-13: You look at premiums paid over the undisturbed share price in similar public deals and apply that range to your target. It only works for public sellers and answers what a buyer would have to offer, not what the company is worth standalone.
valuation-methodologies-14: It works for conglomerates whose divisions deserve different multiples and can reveal a holding-company discount. The downsides: you need segment-level financials, corporate overhead has to be allocated somewhere, and each division needs its own peer set.
valuation-methodologies-15: Build the LBO, then solve for the maximum price a sponsor could pay while still hitting a 20-25% IRR. It gives you a floor on valuation, since a strategic buyer can usually pay more than a sponsor.
valuation-metrics-and-multiples-1: A multiple is shorthand for value ÷ a cash flow proxy — really a compressed version of Value = Cash Flow / (Discount Rate − Growth). It is like price per square foot: it lets you compare assets of different sizes.
valuation-metrics-and-multiples-2: The market expects faster cash flow growth from this company than from its peers. Discount rates rarely differ enough within an industry to explain a five-turn gap.
valuation-metrics-and-multiples-3: EBIT is Operating Income adjusted for non-recurring items; EBITDA is that plus D&A taken from the Cash Flow Statement. Use the Cash Flow Statement figure so you capture all D&A, not just what sits in COGS.
valuation-metrics-and-multiples-4: If the metric is after interest — net income, EPS, levered FCF — pair it with Equity Value. If it is before interest — revenue, EBITDA, EBIT, unlevered FCF — pair it with Enterprise Value.
valuation-metrics-and-multiples-5: EBITDA = $15 EBIT + $5 D&A = $20; TEV = $100 − $20 cash + $40 debt = $120. TEV / EBITDA = 6.0x, with leases excluded on both sides for consistency.
valuation-metrics-and-multiples-6: Under IFRS the rent splits into depreciation and interest, so both EBIT margin and D&A rise and EBITDA is higher. Add the lease liability to Enterprise Value as well, or the multiple is not comparable.
valuation-metrics-and-multiples-7: TEV/EBITDA ignores capital structure and CapEx entirely; TEV/EBIT partially captures CapEx through depreciation, so it is better for capital-intensive businesses; P/E reflects capital structure and taxes, which makes it useless for comparing companies with different leverage.
valuation-metrics-and-multiples-8: Enterprise Value falls, because an operating asset became non-operating cash. The multiple rises, since the asset was sold at 2x against a company trading at 10x.
valuation-metrics-and-multiples-9: Equity Value is unchanged unless the sale books a gain or loss, since net assets are the same. P/E therefore stays flat too, absent that gain.
valuation-metrics-and-multiples-10: Unlevered FCF = NOPAT + D&A ± change in working capital − CapEx, pairs with WACC and Enterprise Value. Levered FCF starts from net income and subtracts mandatory debt repayment, pairs with Cost of Equity and Equity Value.
valuation-metrics-and-multiples-11: Convenience and comparability. EBIT and EBITDA are visible on the face of the statements and are not distorted by financing or one-off working capital swings, so they compare cleanly across companies.
valuation-metrics-and-multiples-12: A spike in CapEx or a large inventory build. Both hit unlevered FCF and neither touches EBITDA — which is exactly why EBITDA overstates cash flow in capital-intensive businesses.
valuation-metrics-and-multiples-14: Enterprise Value = $600 − $100 + $500 = $1,000. Note the mismatch: operations imply $60 of net income while the P/E implies $50, so something non-operating is costing roughly $13 pre-tax.
valuation-metrics-and-multiples-15: (Enterprise Value including all lease liabilities) / EBITDAR, where EBITDAR adds back rent. It neutralizes the US GAAP versus IFRS lease difference that otherwise makes the same company look cheaper or dearer by geography.
discounted-cash-flow-dcf-assumptions-and: Because a company is worth the present value of its future cash flows, and a DCF is the only method that values it on its own fundamentals rather than on what the market pays for someone else.

Project unlevered free cash flow for 5-10 years, discount it at WACC, add the discounted terminal value, and that gives Enterprise Value — then bridge to Equity Value by adding cash and subtracting debt.
Revenue less COGS and OpEx gives EBIT; multiply by (1 − tax rate), add back D&A and other non-cash items, subtract CapEx, and adjust for the change in working capital.

Either apply an exit multiple to final-year EBITDA, or use Gordon Growth: final-year FCF × (1 + g) / (WACC − g). Bankers default to the multiples method and sanity-check it against the growth rate it implies.
You project levered FCF — after interest, debt issuance, and repayment — discount at the Cost of Equity, and get Equity Value directly, skipping the bridge.
No, and they are not supposed to. The unlevered version handles debt through WACC while the levered version handles it inside the cash flows, so the two only converge under textbook assumptions.
No. Unlevered FCF is unaffected, but WACC is not — the debt and equity weights and the levered Beta all change, so you must rerun WACC under the new capital structure.

Unlevered FCF includes only recurring items available to all investors, which is why working capital is in and net interest is out. Interest belongs to one investor group, so it goes into the discount rate instead.
If you deduct an expense in the cash flows, you leave its liability out of the bridge; if you skip the expense, you must subtract the liability. Count it once, in one place.
No — treat SBC as a real expense. It is non-cash but it issues shares and dilutes you, which is a genuine cost to existing owners, unlike a timing difference like D&A.

It is the perpetuity formula: a stream growing at g forever is worth FCF × (1 + g) / (WACC − g). Value rises with growth and falls with the discount rate, and g must stay below WACC or the math breaks.
Public comps, ideally forward multiples, because a standalone valuation should not embed the control premium in precedent transactions. Use precedents only if you are valuing the company in a sale.
Below long-term GDP growth and roughly in line with inflation — typically 1-3% in a developed market. Above GDP means the company eventually becomes the whole economy.
Cross-check the two methods against each other: back into the growth rate your exit multiple implies, and the multiple your growth rate implies. If either looks absurd, your range is wrong.
Yes — a pharma company losing patent exclusivity, or a business in structural decline, can reasonably shrink in perpetuity. The formula still works with negative g.

Simplest approach: treat the entire lease expense as a cash operating cost in the projections, then ignore lease liabilities in both the bridge and WACC. Either capitalize leases everywhere or nowhere.
Growth that never decelerates toward GDP, a terminal value carrying more than about 80% of the total, margins that expand forever, or an implied terminal multiple far off where the comps trade.
Because cash arrives throughout the year, not all on December 31. Discounting at 0.5, 1.5, 2.5 rather than 1, 2, 3 raises the implied value a few percent.
You use one when valuing a company partway through its fiscal year — you discount only the cash flow from today to year-end, not the full year already partly reported.
WACC usually falls at first, because debt is cheaper and tax-deductible, so implied value rises. Push leverage far enough and default risk raises both costs and WACC turns back up.
WACC rises and implied value falls. A higher risk-free rate lifts both the Cost of Equity and the Cost of Debt directly.
The discount rate, by a wide margin. It compounds against every year of cash flow and against the terminal value, which is usually most of the total.
Free cash flow rises because of the lower tax burden, but WACC also rises since the interest tax shield is worth less. The FCF effect normally dominates, so implied value goes up.

The terminal value falls as a share of total value — maybe 50% rather than 70% — which makes the output more defensible. Whether the value itself rises or falls depends on the assumptions in years 11-20.
The emerging-market company gets a higher discount rate from country risk and a higher ERP, so a lower implied value — unless faster growth in the projections more than offsets it.
discounted-cash-flow-dcf-the-discount-ra: The annual return equity investors should expect from the stock over the long run, through price appreciation and dividends. To the company, it is what equity capital costs.
The return you would expect from investing proportionally across the entire capital structure — debt, preferred, and equity. To the company, it is the blended cost of its funding.

Cost of Equity = Risk-Free Rate + Levered Beta × Equity Risk Premium. Use the government bond yield in the currency of the cash flows, and the peer-derived Beta re-levered to the target's capital structure.
Match the currency the cash flows are reported in — 10-year Treasuries for USD, Bunds for EUR, Gilts for GBP. Not the country of operations, the currency of the model.
Weight each country's ERP by the share of revenue earned there and sum the terms. A company with 60% US and 40% Brazil revenue carries a blended premium between the two.
How volatile the stock is relative to the market. Beta of 1.0 moves with the market; 2.0 moves twice as far in both directions; levered Beta includes the extra volatility from debt.
Unlevered Beta = Levered Beta / (1 + D/E × (1 − t)); re-levering reverses it. You strip out each comp's capital structure to isolate business risk, then re-apply your target's.
WACC = Cost of Equity × %E + Cost of Debt × (1 − t) × %D + Cost of Preferred × %P. It pairs with unlevered FCF because both represent all investor groups.
Equity is last in line in a bankruptcy and has no contractual payment, so investors demand more — and unlike interest, dividends are not tax-deductible.
Use the yield to maturity on the company's existing bonds, or the yields on comparable-rated debt if it has none. Both represent what it would pay to issue today, not the coupon it happens to carry.
merger-models-concepts-1: Project both companies, set the purchase price and the cash/debt/stock mix, run sources and uses and purchase price allocation, then combine the income statements with the acquisition effects and compare combined EPS to the buyer's standalone EPS.
merger-models-concepts-2: Accretive if the seller's earnings yield at the purchase price exceeds the buyer's after-tax cost of funding — foregone interest on cash, interest on new debt, and the buyer's own earnings yield on stock.
merger-models-concepts-3: Compare the seller's yield at purchase price (1 / purchase P/E) to the buyer's weighted cost of acquisition. Cost of cash and debt are after-tax rates; cost of stock is 1 / the buyer's P/E.
merger-models-concepts-4: In an all-stock deal, just compare P/E multiples: buyer's P/E above the seller's purchase P/E means accretive, below means dilutive. Cash is cheapest, debt next, stock most expensive.
merger-models-concepts-5: Public sellers: apply a 10-30% premium to the undisturbed share price, benchmarked to premiums in comparable deals. Private sellers: use comps, precedents, and a DCF, since there is no market price to premium off.
merger-models-concepts-6: Purchase Enterprise Value, because that is what the buyer pays all the seller's investors for the core business. Purchase Equity Value is just the cash out the door to shareholders.
merger-models-concepts-7: Cheapest first: excess cash above the minimum balance, then debt up to what the credit markets and the buyer's rating allow, then stock for the remainder. Stock is a last resort because it is the most expensive and signals the buyer thinks its shares are rich.
merger-models-concepts-8: Yes — it means nothing when the buyer is private, has negative EPS, or is a sponsor. Then you look at IRR, cash-on-cash return, contribution analysis, and whether the deal clears the buyer's cost of capital.
merger-models-concepts-9: In a cash-free debt-free deal, the seller's cash and debt both go to zero at close and are replaced with a new minimum cash balance and new deal debt. The buyer effectively buys the enterprise, not the balance sheet.
merger-models-concepts-10: It calculates the goodwill created and the asset write-ups, which keeps the combined balance sheet balanced when the price exceeds the seller's book equity. It also drives the new D&A and any deferred tax liability.
merger-models-concepts-11: In a stock purchase, the write-up of assets is not deductible for cash-tax purposes, so book D&A exceeds tax D&A. That future gap between book and cash taxes is the DTL.
merger-models-concepts-12: Revenue synergies: cross-sell to a share of the buyer's customer base — 1,000 of 100,000 customers buying a $10 product is $10,000. Expense synergies: headcount, facility, and procurement savings you can name and size.
merger-models-concepts-13: Because models often ignore the cost of achieving them — the COGS behind incremental revenue and the one-time integration and severance charges — and assume they arrive immediately rather than phasing in.
merger-models-calculations-3: In an all-stock deal at $150 for $10 of net income, A issues 6 shares, combined EPS is $20 / 16 = $1.25 — 25% accretive. Financed instead: cash at 3% after-tax is accretive against B's 6.7% yield, debt at 7.5% after-tax is dilutive.
merger-models-calculations-4: The after-tax cost of debt must exceed B's 10% yield, so the rate must be above 10% / (1 − 25%) ≈ 13.3%.
merger-models-calculations-5: A's cost of stock is 10% versus B's 8.3% purchase yield, so it is dilutive. B's net income has to reach $120, meaning $20 of after-tax synergies — about $27 pre-tax at a 25% rate.
merger-models-calculations-6: The market wipes out the $200 premium, so A's equity value falls from $2,000 to $1,800 and its share price drops from $10.00 to $9.00.
merger-models-calculations-7: No. The premium disappears regardless of financing — combined equity and enterprise value both fall by the $200 overpayment whether A pays in cash, debt, or stock.
merger-models-calculations-8: Combined Enterprise Value = $600 + $150 = $750M. Combined Equity Value = $500M + $100M of stock issued = $600M.
merger-models-calculations-9: Enterprise Value is unchanged at $750M since financing does not affect it. Equity Value is $500M + $50M of stock = $550M, because the cash half issues no shares.
merger-models-calculations-10: Combined net income is $60M against $600M of equity value, a 10.0x P/E. Combined TEV / EBITDA is $750M / $115M ≈ 6.5x.
merger-models-calculations-11: TEV / EBITDA stays at ~6.5x — financing does not touch it. Net income drops by the $6M after-tax interest to $54M against $500M of equity value, so P/E goes to ~9.3x.
merger-models-calculations-12: Enterprise-value multiples always land between the buyer's and the purchase multiple, since both numerator and denominator simply add. Equity-value multiples usually do but need not, because financing changes the combined equity value.
lbo-models-concepts-1: A sponsor buys a company using mostly debt, uses the company's own cash flow to pay that debt down, and sells in three to seven years. It works because leverage magnifies the return on a smaller equity check, and interest is tax-deductible.
lbo-models-concepts-2: Set entry assumptions and build sources and uses to solve for the equity check; project EBITDA and free cash flow; run the debt schedule with mandatory amortization and a cash sweep; then exit at an assumed multiple and compute equity proceeds, MOIC, and IRR.
lbo-models-concepts-3: Entry and exit multiples matter most, then leverage, then EBITDA growth. Buy cheap and sell dear beats almost anything you can do operationally.
lbo-models-concepts-4: Assume a premium to the current share price and check the implied multiple against comps, precedents, and the DCF. Exit multiple is conventionally set at or below entry — assuming expansion is how you talk yourself into a bad deal.
lbo-models-concepts-5: Stable, predictable cash flow above all, plus low CapEx and working capital needs, a defensible market position, an unlevered balance sheet, and a credible exit. At the right price almost anything works.
lbo-models-concepts-6: FCF = net income + D&A ± change in working capital − CapEx, or EBITDA − cash interest − cash taxes ± working capital − CapEx. EBITDA ignores interest, taxes, and CapEx, which is exactly what determines whether the debt gets paid.
lbo-models-concepts-7: Cash available for debt repayment = beginning cash + FCF − minimum cash. They are not the same because the company has to hold a minimum cash balance and starts each year with a different balance.
lbo-models-concepts-8: Sale to a strategic, sale to another sponsor, or an IPO. Most firms prefer a sale to a strategic, since it is a clean full exit at the highest price; an IPO only sells down a stake over time.
lbo-models-concepts-9: Buy cheaper or sell higher, grow EBITDA through revenue and margins, use more leverage or pay down debt faster, and pull returns forward with a dividend recap or an earlier exit.
lbo-models-concepts-10: Look at Debt / EBITDA in recent comparable LBOs and at leveraged public peers — typically 4-6x total in a normal market. Tranche count follows the size: a revolver and term loan B for smaller deals, adding second lien or high-yield for larger ones.
lbo-models-concepts-11: Secured bank debt — revolver and term loans, cheapest, amortizing, covenant-heavy — then unsecured high-yield bonds, then mezzanine or PIK. Cost rises and security falls as you go down the stack.
lbo-models-concepts-12: It is the plug for cash shortfalls: draw when free cash flow cannot cover mandatory repayments and the minimum cash balance, and repay it first when cash is available. It is usually undrawn at close and carries a commitment fee.
lbo-models-concepts-13: Mandatory is MIN(amortization % × original principal, remaining balance) for each tranche. Optional is the cash sweep — leftover cash after mandatory payments and minimum cash, applied to the most senior tranche first.
lbo-models-concepts-14: Set a target IRR, usually 20-25%, and solve for the price that achieves it. That price is a floor, because a strategic buyer with synergies and a lower return hurdle can always pay more.
lbo-models-concepts-15: It depends on the time frame. A 50% IRR over six months is barely any money; a 3.0x over ten years is a mediocre annualized return. Funds are judged on IRR but LPs get paid in dollars.
lbo-models-calculations-1: Equity in is $400M; exit enterprise value is $1,350M less $350M of remaining debt, so $1,000M out. That is 2.5x over five years, roughly a 20% IRR.
lbo-models-calculations-2: Equity is $700M and a 25% IRR over five years needs ~3.0x, so $2,100M of proceeds. Debt stays at $500M, so exit enterprise value must be $2,600M — a 13.0x multiple on $200M of EBITDA.
lbo-models-calculations-3: With $375M repaid, $125M of debt remains, so exit enterprise value only needs to be $2,225M for the same $2,100M of proceeds — about 11.1x.
lbo-models-calculations-4: A 20% IRR over five years is ~2.5x, so $500M of equity must return $1,250M. Exit enterprise value is $1,650M, leaving $400M of debt — so only $100M gets repaid.
lbo-models-calculations-5: Equity is $400M and 25% over five years needs ~3.0x, so $1,200M of proceeds against $300M of remaining debt. Exit enterprise value must be $1,500M — a 10.0x multiple on $150M of EBITDA.
pe-lbo-drill-1: Five steps: transaction assumptions and sources and uses, opening balance sheet adjustments, the operating projections, the debt schedule with mandatory amortization and cash sweep, then exit and returns.
pe-lbo-drill-2: Three drivers: EBITDA growth, debt paydown, and multiple expansion. Only the first genuinely creates value, which is why sponsors underwrite flat exit multiples and treat expansion as upside.
pe-lbo-drill-3: Debt is cheaper than equity — senior, secured, and tax-deductible — so replacing equity with it raises the return on the equity that remains. Leverage magnifies both directions, which is why cash flow stability matters more than growth.
pe-lbo-drill-4: Stable, predictable free cash flow first, then low CapEx and working capital intensity, a defensible position, an unlevered balance sheet, and a clear exit at a sane entry price.
pe-lbo-drill-5: Uses are everything you pay for — equity purchase price, refinanced debt, fees. Sources are the funding — each debt tranche, rollover equity, and sponsor equity as the plug that makes the two sides equal.
pe-lbo-drill-6: What the credit market will actually fund, not what maximizes IRR: check leverage multiples on comparable deals, interest coverage above ~2.0x, and whether the company still services its debt in a downside case.
pe-lbo-drill-7: Start from free cash flow available for debt repayment, take mandatory amortization first, then sweep whatever is left against the most senior tranche. Ending debt feeds next year's interest, which is the circularity in the model.
pe-lbo-drill-8: Revolver, term loan A, term loan B, then second lien, high-yield bonds, mezzanine or PIK, and preferred or common equity at the bottom. Cost rises and security falls with every rung down.
pe-lbo-drill-9: A maintenance covenant is tested every quarter no matter what the company does; an incurrence covenant is only tested when the company takes an action, like raising debt or paying a dividend. Bank debt carries maintenance, bonds carry incurrence.
pe-lbo-drill-10: PIK interest accrues onto the principal instead of being paid in cash, so the balance compounds. Sponsors use it to protect near-term cash flow, usually at a 75-100bp premium to the cash rate.
pe-lbo-drill-11: The company raises new debt and pays the proceeds to the sponsor as a dividend without selling anything. It pulls IRR forward by returning capital early, but adds leverage and risk without creating any value.
pe-lbo-drill-12: MOIC is cash out over cash in and ignores time; IRR is time-weighted. They diverge on short holds — a fast 1.5x can beat a slow 3.0x on IRR — and any early distribution flatters IRR without changing MOIC.
pe-lbo-drill-13: The grid worth memorizing: 2.0x is ~26% over 3 years, ~19% over 4, ~15% over 5. 2.5x is ~36% / ~26% / ~20%. 3.0x is ~44% / ~32% / ~25%.
pe-lbo-drill-14: MOIC = $525 / $200 = 2.6x. Between the 2.0x (~15%) and 3.0x (~25%) five-year anchors, that is roughly a 21% IRR.
pe-lbo-drill-15: Equity in is $200M; exit equity is $675M − $150M of debt = $525M. That is 2.6x, or about a 21% IRR over five years.
pe-lbo-drill-16: Equity in is $500M; exit equity is $1,280M − $300M = $980M, so ~2.0x and a 14-15% IRR. That misses a 20% hurdle, so the deal needs a cheaper entry, more leverage, or faster growth.
pe-lbo-drill-17: Equity in is $300M; roughly $190M of cumulative free cash flow leaves $310M of debt, and exit enterprise value is 8x × $128M = $1,022M. Equity out is $712M — 2.4x and about a 19% IRR.
pe-lbo-drill-18: Six lines: entry EV, debt and equity, exit EBITDA, exit EV, remaining debt, then equity proceeds and MOIC converted to IRR from the grid. Round hard and say your assumptions out loud.
pe-lbo-drill-19: The exit multiple. A turn of leverage saves $100M of equity but costs interest, so it is worth 2-4 points of IRR; a turn of exit multiple on $130M of EBITDA is $130M of free equity value — and you control leverage, not the exit.
pe-lbo-drill-20: Zero. Enterprise value and net debt are both unchanged, so the equity check comes back at 1.0x — slightly negative after fees. Leverage alone creates nothing.
pe-lbo-drill-21: A DCF discounts unlevered cash flow at WACC to find intrinsic value; an LBO solves for the price a sponsor can pay to hit a target return. One tells you what it is worth, the other what you can bid.
pe-lbo-drill-22: Goodwill is the plug that balances the opening balance sheet — purchase equity price less the target's book equity, adjusted for write-ups and existing goodwill. It does not affect returns, since returns run off cash flow and the exit multiple.
pe-lbo-drill-23: Shift the burden forward with seller notes, earnouts, or PIK preferred; use asset-based or sale-leaseback financing against the balance sheet; or accept lower leverage and underwrite the deal on growth rather than debt paydown.
pe-lbo-drill-24: Compare them in the downside case, not the base case. More leverage almost always wins on base-case IRR; the question is which structure still services its debt in a recession.
pe-lbo-drill-25: A ~2% management fee on committed capital, stepping down to invested capital, which covers overhead; and 20% carried interest on profits above an 8% preferred return. Carry is the real economics.
pe-lbo-drill-26: Gross IRR is measured at the deal level, before fund costs; net IRR is what the LP actually keeps after fees, carry, expenses, and any subscription line effect. The gap is typically 5-10 points.
pe-lbo-drill-27: Sourcing and screen, CIM and a quick model for the first-round bid, management meetings and full diligence, financing commitments, final bid and purchase agreement, then signing and close.
pe-lbo-drill-28: Work top-down to kill it fast: the market's growth and durability, the company's competitive position, quality and recurrence of the earnings, cash conversion and leverage capacity, then whether a plausible entry price clears your return hurdle.
pe-lbo-drill-29: Ownership rather than execution — you live with the decision for five years instead of moving on at close — plus judgment over process and a longer feedback loop. Back each with something you have actually done.
pe-lbo-drill-30: Five parts in two minutes: what the company does, why it is a good LBO candidate, the thesis and value creation plan, the returns math at a stated entry and exit, and the two risks that would break it.
pe-lbo-drill-31: A QofE is accounting diligence that tests whether reported EBITDA is real, recurring, and sustainable — scrubbing add-backs, normalizing working capital, and checking revenue recognition. Every deal has one because the purchase price is a multiple of that number.
pe-lbo-drill-32: Direction and consequence. On the sell side you build the story to support a price; in PE you try to break it before committing capital you cannot recover for five to seven years.
debt-capital-markets-dcm-leveraged-finan: Debt is cheaper, tax-deductible, and does not dilute owners. It fits mature companies with stable cash flow and credit stats that support it; growth companies with volatile cash flow should issue equity.

Compare the after-tax cost of each, how WACC moves under both, and what the credit stats look like after. Mature, stable, and under-levered points to debt; high-growth or already stretched points to equity.

The utility takes 100% debt — regulated, predictable cash flow. The railroad takes 50/50, capital-intensive but cyclical. The branded pharma takes 100% equity, since patent cliffs and R&D make cash flow too uncertain for lenders.

Start with the cheapest — term loans — and stress the maintenance covenants across scenarios. If the company breaches covenants in a downside case, move to subordinated notes, which cost more but carry only incurrence covenants.
DSCR includes CapEx, taxes, and principal amortization, which the EBITDA-based ratios ignore. Fix it by cutting CapEx, extending the amortization schedule, or refinancing into a bullet structure.
Give lenders yield somewhere other than the coupon: an original issue discount, warrants, a PIK component, or tighter covenants and call protection. The yield stays; the cash interest falls.
Material moves in credit stats like Debt / EBITDA or EBITDA / Interest relative to rated peers, or qualitative shifts — a big acquisition, an industry downturn, or a change in financial policy.

Coupon rate is fixed interest on par. Current yield is coupon / market price. YTM is the total annualized return if held to maturity, including the pull to par — the only one that reflects what you actually earn.
Discount the coupons and the principal repayment back at the appropriate yield and add them up. The discount rate comes from yields on comparable-rated bonds of similar maturity.
Approximate YTM = (annual interest + (par − price) / years) / ((par + price) / 2) = ($8 + $1) / $97.50 ≈ 9.2%.
The 5% bond. Less of its value comes back as coupons, so more of it sits in the final principal repayment — longer duration, more price sensitivity.

Duration is the first-order price sensitivity to a change in yield; convexity is the curvature correction. Together they tell you how much a bond moves for a 1% rate change, and convexity means gains from falling rates exceed losses from rising ones.
Duration. Moving from a 7-year 8% bond to a 10-year 6% bond materially lengthens duration, so investors take much more interest-rate risk and will demand a higher yield than 6%.

Yield to Worst is the lowest of the yield to maturity and the yields to each call date — what you earn if the issuer exercises its most disadvantageous option. For a callable bond trading above par, YTW is usually the yield to the earliest call.

Screen by industry, geography, size, date, and rating, then compare coupon, yield to maturity, spread over the benchmark, tenor, seniority, and covenant package. The spread at issuance is what prices your deal.
distressed-restructuring-1: It combines M&A, valuation, credit, and bankruptcy law, the outcomes are genuinely uncertain, and the technical work is harder than in coverage. It is also counter-cyclical, which means deal flow when everyone else has none.
distressed-restructuring-2: Debtor side (the company) or creditor side (the lenders). Debtor mandates are usually larger and better paid; creditor mandates are more numerous. Know which side the firm you are interviewing with typically takes.
distressed-restructuring-3: Stressed: still paying interest but facing a maturity wall or cash crunch. Distressed: already missed a payment or breached a covenant. Bankrupt: filed for Chapter 11 or Chapter 7.
distressed-restructuring-4: Macro shocks — an industry downturn, a commodity move, a pandemic — or micro failures like over-expansion, a bad acquisition, an over-levered LBO, or losing a key customer. Usually a leveraged balance sheet plus one shock.
distressed-restructuring-5: Refinance, sell assets, negotiate an out-of-court restructuring, or file Chapter 11. Out-of-court is faster and cheaper but needs near-unanimous creditor consent; Chapter 11 binds holdouts but is slow, expensive, and public.
distressed-restructuring-6: Chapter 7 is liquidation — a trustee sells the assets and distributes proceeds. Chapter 11 is reorganization — the company keeps operating as debtor-in-possession and emerges with a restructured balance sheet.
distressed-restructuring-7: New money lent to a company already in Chapter 11 that primes every existing claim, including secured debt. It is the safest paper in the capital structure, which is why lenders will fund a company nobody else will touch.
distressed-restructuring-8: A court-supervised asset sale inside Chapter 11 that delivers assets free and clear of liens, with a stalking-horse bid setting the floor and an auction on top. It is faster than a plan of reorganization and gets buyers past successor liability.
distressed-restructuring-9: A weekly forecast of cash receipts and disbursements, granular enough to show exactly when the company runs out of money. It is the operating document in a restructuring — it drives DIP sizing and the negotiation timeline.
distressed-restructuring-10: You use the same methodologies but at the low end of the range, lean harder on liquidation value as a floor, and add scenarios for restructuring outcomes. The real question shifts from company value to where the fulcrum security sits.
distressed-restructuring-11: Apply a recovery percentage to each asset's book value — cash near 100%, receivables and inventory 50-90%, PP&E and intangibles far less — then pay claims down the waterfall by seniority until the proceeds run out.
distressed-restructuring-12: Proceeds are $300 of enterprise value plus $50 of cash = $350. The revolver recovers 100%, the term loan takes the remaining $250 for an 83% recovery, and the subordinated notes get zero.
distressed-restructuring-13: Each subsidiary's debt is paid from its own enterprise value first: A recovers 100%, B's lenders take $50 for 50%, C recovers 100%. HoldCo gets only the residual equity from A and C — $80 plus $50 = $130 — so its $100 recovers in full.
distressed-restructuring-14: A healthy 5x on $50 of EBITDA is $250, covering both tranches, but distress compresses the multiple. Around 3x the secured notes still recover fully near par while the unsecured trade at a steep discount — they are the fulcrum.
distressed-restructuring-15: The high YTM is fictional if the company cannot pay. Value the debt on recovery instead: estimate distressed enterprise value, walk the waterfall, and see what this tranche actually gets in a restructuring.
equity-capital-markets-ecm-1: Apply a range of forward multiples to projected metrics to get post-money value, subtract the IPO discount, then solve for the primary shares issued to raise the target proceeds and the resulting ownership split.
equity-capital-markets-ecm-2: Correct — the valuation comes from the comps. The model determines share count, the IPO discount, proceeds, and post-deal ownership percentages, not the value itself.
equity-capital-markets-ecm-3: Primary shares are newly issued and the cash goes to the company, diluting existing holders. Secondary shares are existing holders selling — no dilution, no new capital, and the cash goes to them.
equity-capital-markets-ecm-4: It lets underwriters sell up to 15% more shares. They use it when demand is strong, and it also gives them a mechanism to support the stock after pricing by covering their short.
equity-capital-markets-ecm-5: The current share price anchors it, not comps: you set a discount to the market price, and shares issued follow from the capital being raised. Then measure the dilution to EPS and ownership.
equity-capital-markets-ecm-6: A sponsor takes an empty shell public at $10 a share, holds the cash in trust, then merges with a private target — which becomes public — usually alongside a PIPE to top up the cash after redemptions.
equity-capital-markets-ecm-7: SPACs are faster, lighter on regulation, and let the target negotiate a price and give forward projections. The costs: sponsor promote of ~20%, redemption risk that guts the cash, and worse post-deal trading performance.
equity-capital-markets-ecm-8: Partially correct. The market price does stay above the payoff value above the conversion price, because of the option value and downside protection — but that premium narrows as the stock rises far above it.
equity-capital-markets-ecm-9: The cash coupon is lower, but you are selling an equity option — if the stock rises, conversion dilutes existing shareholders at a below-market price. That embedded option is the real cost.
equity-capital-markets-ecm-10: Because you pay a conversion premium — usually 20-30% — for the same eventual shares, and you give up dividends and full upside participation in exchange for that downside protection.
financial-institutions-group-fig-1: Banks earn a spread between the interest on loans and the cost of deposits and debt, so debt is operating rather than financing. That kills Enterprise Value, EBITDA, and unlevered DCFs — you value them on Equity Value with P/E, P/BV, and a dividend discount model.
financial-institutions-group-fig-2: Same equity-only framework, but the projections start from premiums rather than the balance sheet: premiums written and earned, claims and expenses, and investment income on the float.
financial-institutions-group-fig-3: Specialty finance works like a bank on spread with lighter regulation; asset managers are fee-on-AUM businesses valued on normal multiples; broker-dealers earn commissions and trading revenue; fintech is usually valued like software.
financial-institutions-group-fig-4: ROE drives P/BV, and ROTCE drives P/TBV — the same way growth drives TEV/EBITDA for normal companies. A bank earning above its cost of equity trades above book value.
financial-institutions-group-fig-5: The buffer of loss-absorbing capital that regulators require against unexpected losses, on top of the reserves for expected ones. It caps how much a bank can lend and how much it can pay out.
financial-institutions-group-fig-6: CET1 is common equity less goodwill and intangibles, the purest loss-absorbing capital. The CET1 ratio is CET1 / risk-weighted assets, and regulators set the minimum a bank must hold.
financial-institutions-group-fig-7: A $100 provision cuts pre-tax income by $100 and net income by $75, and the Allowance for Loan Losses rises so net loans fall $100. CET1 falls with retained earnings, so the CET1 ratio drops.
financial-institutions-group-fig-8: Only $40 of the $100 written is earned revenue, but the full $10 commission is paid in cash. The unearned portion sits as Deferred Acquisition Costs on the balance sheet and amortizes as the premium is earned.
financial-institutions-group-fig-9: Combined Ratio = Loss & LAE Ratio + Expense Ratio. Below 100% means the insurer makes money on underwriting alone; above 100% means it needs investment income on the float to be profitable.
financial-institutions-group-fig-10: Start with the balance sheet — loans, deposits, and other interest-earning assets — apply rates to get net interest income, add fee income, subtract provisions and expenses, then check the result against regulatory capital requirements.
financial-institutions-group-fig-11: LCR = high-quality liquid assets / stressed 30-day net outflows, minimum 100% — can the bank survive a month-long run. NSFR = available / required stable funding over one year — is the funding profile durable.
financial-institutions-group-fig-12: Grow assets and risk-weighted assets, apply an ROA to get net income, then pay out whatever exceeds the bank's target CET1 ratio as dividends. Discount those dividends at the Cost of Equity and add a terminal value.
financial-institutions-group-fig-13: Embedded Value = Net Asset Value + the present value of future profits from policies already written. It values the existing book only, which is why you add new-business value separately to get appraisal value.
financial-institutions-group-fig-14: P&C writes short-tail policies repriced annually, so claims come quickly and reserves are short. Life writes decades-long contracts, so its float is far larger and duration matching and interest rates matter much more.
financial-institutions-group-fig-15: Deals are almost always all-stock, there is no enterprise value or EBITDA, and purchase accounting marks the loan book to fair value. You also model the pro-forma regulatory capital ratios, which can gate the deal entirely.
financial-sponsors-group-fsg-1: AUM, fee-related earnings, and distributable earnings, valued on P/FRE, P/DE, and TEV/AUM. Split management fees from carry: fee income is a stable annuity, carry is volatile and deserves a lower multiple.
financial-sponsors-group-fsg-2: Because the earnings streams differ even if the strategy does not: management fees are contractual and predictable, carried interest is levered to performance. You value each at its own multiple and add them.
financial-sponsors-group-fsg-3: When the asset is at year five to seven of the hold, the value creation plan is largely done, the next fundraise needs realizations, and the M&A or IPO window is open.
financial-sponsors-group-fsg-4: When they are about to raise the next fund — LPs will not commit to a new vehicle while the current one still has significant dry powder, and the investment period may be about to expire.
financial-sponsors-group-fsg-5: Carve-outs from a corporate parent, take-privates of public companies, growth equity minority stakes, add-on acquisitions for existing platforms, and secondary buyouts from another sponsor.
private-capital-advisory-secondaries-1: LP-led: an investor sells its stake in an existing fund to a buyer, usually at a discount to NAV. GP-led: the manager moves one or more assets into a continuation vehicle, giving existing LPs a choice to cash out or roll.
private-capital-advisory-secondaries-2: With only 0.2x realized, pricing hangs on the credibility of the marks — the fund's vintage and stage, the quality and concentration of the remaining assets, the mark-to-comps gap, and remaining fees.
private-capital-advisory-secondaries-3: The denominator effect after public markets fall, portfolio rebalancing, liquidity needs, a change in strategy or manager relationship, or simply wanting to avoid future capital calls.
private-capital-advisory-secondaries-4: To hold a strong asset past the fund's life while returning capital to existing LPs, and to keep compounding an asset they know well rather than sell into a weak market. It also generates realized DPI ahead of the next fundraise.
private-capital-advisory-secondaries-5: GP-led deals run like sell-side M&A — marketing materials, diligence, buyer outreach — so fees are high. LP-led deals are more like brokerage: faster, more commoditized, and priced off NAV with lower fees.
private-companies-1: No public market, so no share price and far less liquidity; reporting is non-standard, often cash-basis or tax-optimized; ownership is concentrated and often mixed with personal expenses.
private-companies-2: Normalize owner compensation to market rates, strip out personal expenses run through the business, restate to accrual accounting, and remove non-recurring items. You are rebuilding the EBITDA a buyer would actually get.
private-companies-3: Same methodologies, then discounts: an illiquidity discount of 10-30%, no control premium reference from a share price, and a higher discount rate for size and concentration risk.
private-companies-4: The risk-free rate and ERP are unchanged, but Beta comes from comparable public companies re-levered to the target's structure, and you add a size premium. Use a target capital structure, since there is no market value of equity.
private-companies-5: There is no share price to premium off, so valuation runs on comps and a DCF; deals are often cash-free debt-free asset purchases with a step-up in tax basis, escrows, earnouts, and heavier diligence on the numbers.
consumer-retail-1: Staples versus discretionary, plus pure-play retailers. Staples get higher multiples for predictable demand; discretionary is cyclical and cheaper; retailers are asset-heavy and lease-laden, so they trade lowest.
consumer-retail-2: Franchise, and by a wide margin. Franchising is capital-light royalty income with high margins and no store CapEx, so more EBITDA converts to cash and the multiple is higher.
consumer-retail-3: Store count, sales per store, same-store sales growth, and sales per square foot on the revenue side; gross margin, occupancy cost, and new-store CapEx below it.
consumer-retail-4: Store-level EBITDA — revenue less COGS and store operating costs, before any corporate overhead. It shows whether the individual store economics work, separate from head-office cost.
consumer-retail-5: When the set mixes US GAAP and IFRS companies. EBITDAR adds rent back, so lease treatment stops distorting the comparison — pair it with an enterprise value that includes lease liabilities.
healthcare-biotech-1: Pharma, biotech and life sciences, and healthcare equipment and services. Commercial pharma and equipment get standard DCF and EBITDA multiples; clinical-stage biotech needs probability-adjusted, drug-by-drug NPV.
healthcare-biotech-2: Build a probability-adjusted DCF per drug: forecast R&D through each remaining trial phase, multiply by the probability of passing each one, then model post-approval revenue to patent expiry and discount at 10-15%.
healthcare-biotech-3: Only marginally. Multiples need revenue, so pre-revenue companies get valued on TEV per pipeline drug or per patient population — mostly you rely on risk-adjusted NPV and recent financing rounds.
healthcare-biotech-4: You use a standard DCF and normal multiples for the marketed drugs, then bolt on a probability-adjusted pipeline valued separately. Split by patent expiry so the cliff shows up explicitly.
healthcare-biotech-5: Model it like a retailer: facilities × beds × occupancy × revenue per bed, with payor mix driving realized rates. Costs are mostly labor, and CapEx is maintenance plus new facilities.
industrials-1: It makes and moves physical products for corporate and government buyers, so it is capital-intensive, highly cyclical, and backlog-driven. Verticals span aerospace and defense, machinery, transportation, and building products.
industrials-2: Start with capacity — available seat miles — then load factor to get traffic, and yield per mile for revenue. Costs run on cost per available seat mile, with fuel and labor dominating and fleet CapEx below.
industrials-3: Many are GP/LP structures with distributions rather than earnings, vessels are valued at market on a per-ship basis, and charter rates are volatile — so NAV per vessel matters more than EBITDA multiples.
industrials-4: Backlog becomes the key metric, with book-to-bill (order intake / revenue recognized) as the leading indicator. Revenue is recognized over time as work progresses, so cash collection and reported revenue diverge.
industrials-5: Most useful for conglomerates with genuinely different segments and for shippers with mixed fleets. Least useful for a single-product manufacturer where segments share cost structure and customers.
metals-mining-1: Split by metal — base and bulk, precious, diversified — or by stage: producers, developers, and explorers. Producers get cash-flow multiples; developers and explorers get NAV and TEV per reserve.
metals-mining-2: Forecast on production capacity, utilization, and realized steel prices, with a gross margin per ton. Value on TEV/EBITDA and a DCF, since a processor has no orebody to run a NAV against.
metals-mining-3: It depends. TEV/NOPAT reflects tax differences and captures capital intensity through depreciation, which matters in mining — but EBITDA multiples are more comparable across jurisdictions. Show both.
metals-mining-4: Value developed mines by discounting production to depletion, then add undeveloped projects at a risk-adjusted DCF net of development CapEx. Sum them, subtract net debt and corporate costs, and compare to market cap as P/NAV.
metals-mining-5: Reserves are economically recoverable — proved and probable. Resources are the broader geological estimate — measured, indicated, then inferred, in falling order of confidence. Only reserves belong in a NAV without heavy discounting.
metals-mining-6: P/NAV, TEV/Reserves, TEV/Resources, and P/CF. Mines are depleting assets with finite lives, so per-unit reserve value tells you more than an earnings multiple on a single cyclical year.
metals-mining-7: Gold miners trade at a premium P/NAV, often above 1.0x, because gold is treated as a store of value and investors buy miners for leveraged commodity exposure. Copper is industrial and cyclical, so it trades below.
metals-mining-8: They convert a multi-metal production profile into one comparable unit using relative prices, so you can compare miners with different metal mixes on a single per-unit basis.
metals-mining-9: Screen on reserves, resources, or annual production instead of revenue or EBITDA, plus jurisdiction and metal mix. Commodity price swings make financial-metric screens useless in this sector.
metals-mining-10: No. NAV is decades of future cash flow while NAV growth measures a year or two, so short-term changes say little about the multiple. Commodity price expectations and jurisdiction risk drive P/NAV far more.
oil-gas-1: Upstream (E&P), midstream, downstream, oilfield services, and integrateds. E&P is valued on NAV and per-flowing-barrel metrics, midstream on EV/EBITDA and distributions, downstream on crack spreads and normal multiples.
oil-gas-2: Decline existing production until proved developed reserves are uneconomic, add undeveloped locations with their drilling CapEx, apply a strip or flat price deck, discount at 10%, then subtract net debt and corporate costs.
oil-gas-3: Upfront cost is 80% of $10M = $8M. Production starts at 365,000 barrels a year and declines 20% annually until the 1 million barrel EUR is exhausted; take 80% working interest less the 10% royalty on revenue, subtract operating costs, and IRR that stream against the $8M.
oil-gas-4: Probably not. A 7.0 reserve life ratio and 80% production replacement means the company is shrinking, so its internal NAV is likely giving credit to probable and possible reserves the market will not pay for.
oil-gas-5: Successful efforts expenses failed exploration immediately; full cost capitalizes it and amortizes it. Full cost shows higher earnings and assets, so you normalize before comparing companies on P/E or book value.
oil-gas-6: Annual production is 600 MMcf plus 50 MBbl × 6 = 300 MMcf, so 900 MMcfe. Reserve life = 10 Bcfe / 0.9 Bcfe ≈ 11 years.
oil-gas-7: Screen on proved reserves, production, and basin rather than revenue or EBITDA, since commodity prices make financial metrics swing wildly. Also match oil-versus-gas mix and hedging position.
oil-gas-8: It is a toll business: capacity × utilization × fee per unit, with contracted volumes and inflation escalators. Value on EV/EBITDA and distributable cash flow, since throughput contracts make the cash flow bond-like.
oil-gas-9: MLPs pay no corporate tax and distribute nearly all cash flow, so investors value them on yield and distributable cash flow per unit rather than P/E, and the GP's incentive distribution rights take a growing share of cash.
oil-gas-10: Standard DCF and EV/EBITDA, but the forecast runs on refinery count, capacity, utilization, and the crack spread — the margin between crude cost and refined product prices, which is the whole business.
power-utilities-1: Regulated utilities, unregulated independent power producers, and multi-utilities. Regulated names are valued on rate base growth and allowed ROE; IPPs are normal companies exposed to merchant power prices.
power-utilities-2: Equity is $1,000, so allowed net income at 12% is $120, or $160 pre-tax. Add $60 of interest, $60 of O&M, and $20 of depreciation for a $300M revenue requirement — $300M / 1,500 GWh = $0.20 per kWh.
power-utilities-3: They value the asset base and physical capacity independently of capital structure, operating efficiency, and local rate regulation — which is exactly what differs across utilities and makes EBITDA multiples hard to compare.
power-utilities-4: You cannot answer without each segment's rate base, capital structure, and authorized ROE. Generally the segment with the highest allowed ROE earns the highest multiple, since it converts rate base into earnings fastest.
power-utilities-5: It depends on power prices. When prices are high the IPP earns more than an authorized ROE would allow and trades up; when they are low it trades at a discount for the volatility. Regulated names are steadier and hold their multiple.
project-finance-infrastructure-1: Project finance lends against a single asset's contracted cash flows through a ring-fenced SPV, non-recourse to the sponsor. Corporate finance lends against the whole company's balance sheet and credit.
project-finance-infrastructure-2: Set the purchase price and timeline, forecast revenue and expenses from the asset's contracted drivers, size the debt off the cash flows, then compute equity IRR through an exit or an assumed hold to end of life.
project-finance-infrastructure-3: You add a construction phase: capitalized construction costs, debt and equity drawn over time, and interest during construction rolled into principal. No revenue until commercial operation, so the equity IRR is more back-ended and riskier.
project-finance-infrastructure-4: Revenue is capacity in MW × hours × capacity factor × the contracted or merchant price per MWh. Costs split into fuel, which passes through under a tolling agreement, and fixed O&M plus maintenance CapEx.
project-finance-infrastructure-5: The PPA solar plant is the safest and lowest-returning — contracted price and volume. Merchant solar carries price risk. The airport carries volume, GDP, and regulatory risk, so highest risk and highest potential return.
project-finance-infrastructure-6: Because contracted cash flows are predictable, so you can set debt service to a target coverage ratio in every period rather than a flat amortization. That maximizes leverage without ever breaching the DSCR.
project-finance-infrastructure-7: DSCR = cash flow available for debt service / total debt service in each period; LLCR = present value of cash flow over the loan life / debt outstanding. You size the loan so both clear their minimums, typically 1.3-1.5x.
project-finance-infrastructure-8: Circularity: interest depends on the debt balance, and the sculpted debt balance depends on after-tax cash flow, which depends on interest. You break it with iterative calculation or a manual copy-paste loop.
project-finance-infrastructure-9: Build downside cases for the things that actually break the asset — lower resource or volume, delayed completion, higher operating cost, counterparty default — and size the debt so the DSCR still holds in that case.
project-finance-infrastructure-10: Fees and interest during construction are capitalized into the loan, but the loan size depends on those fees. Break it by iterative calculation, a hardcoded fee estimate, or a copy-paste macro.
real-estate-properties-1: Office, industrial, retail, and multifamily, plus hotels, data centers, and healthcare. Office, industrial, and retail run on long leases with predictable cash flow; multifamily and hotels reprice constantly, so hotels are the most volatile.
real-estate-properties-2: NOI is rental revenue less operating expenses, before debt service, taxes, and capital costs — the property-level equivalent of EBITDA. It is the number cap rates are quoted against, which makes it the basis of every valuation.
real-estate-properties-3: Cap Rate = stabilized forward NOI / property value — the unlevered yield, and the real estate version of an inverse multiple. Low cap rates mean expensive, high-quality, low-risk assets.
real-estate-properties-4: Because NOI margins run above 50%, cash flow is stable and contractually locked in through leases, CapEx is low, and the debt is secured by a hard asset with a liquid market. Lenders take real estate risk far more comfortably than business risk.
real-estate-properties-5: Start at base rental income at full occupancy, subtract vacancy and concessions, add expense reimbursements to get effective gross income, subtract operating expenses for NOI, then subtract capital costs and debt service to get cash flow to equity.
real-estate-properties-6: NOI is before capital costs and debt service; Adjusted NOI subtracts leasing commissions, tenant improvements, and reserves; Cash Flow to Equity subtracts debt service on top. Each is one step closer to what the owner actually pockets.
real-estate-properties-7: Model the land purchase and construction spend over the build period with debt drawn alongside equity, then lease-up to stabilization, then a sale at a cap rate on stabilized NOI. Returns come from the spread between development cost and stabilized value.
real-estate-properties-8: Buy at a cap rate on stabilized NOI with a set debt and equity split, project rent growth and expenses through the hold, subtract debt service, then exit at a cap rate — usually assumed slightly above entry.
real-estate-properties-9: Cap rate on stabilized NOI, a DCF of property cash flows, and replacement cost. Cap rates dominate in practice; replacement cost is the sanity check on whether new supply is coming.
real-estate-properties-10: Equity proceeds are split disproportionately: investors get their capital back plus a preferred return first, then the developer takes an outsized promote above each IRR hurdle. It pays the sponsor for performance rather than for capital contributed.
real-estate-investment-trusts-reits-1: A REIT must distribute 90% of taxable income as dividends and hold mostly real estate assets and income, and in exchange it pays no corporate tax. Distributing everything means it constantly returns to capital markets to fund growth.
real-estate-investment-trusts-reits-2: Use P/FFO and P/AFFO rather than P/E, plus a NAV model built from property-level NOI capped at market rates, and a dividend discount model. Depreciation makes net income and P/E close to meaningless.
real-estate-investment-trusts-reits-3: Cap each property segment's NOI at a market cap rate, sum the values, add other assets, subtract debt, and divide by share count. It matters for US REITs because they carry properties at depreciated cost, not fair value.
real-estate-investment-trusts-reits-4: IFRS REITs mark properties to fair value through the income statement each year; US REITs carry them at historical cost less depreciation. That is why NAV models matter more in the US and why IFRS earnings swing with property values.
real-estate-investment-trusts-reits-5: FFO = net income + real estate depreciation − gains on property sales. It strips out the depreciation and one-off gains that make REIT net income meaningless; AFFO goes further by subtracting maintenance CapEx and leasing costs.
real-estate-investment-trusts-reits-6: The unlevered DCF is quickest but least natural for a business where debt is permanent. The DDM fits the 90% payout requirement, and the levered DCF gets closest to equity cash flow — both need explicit debt and equity issuance forecasts.
real-estate-investment-trusts-reits-7: Raise debt up to the covenant and rating limits since it is cheaper, then issue equity — which REITs do far more often than normal companies, because the 90% payout rule leaves no retained cash to fund growth.
real-estate-investment-trusts-reits-8: Mostly all-stock, since REITs hold little cash and are already levered. The price is set on NAV per share and P/FFO rather than EPS accretion, and both sides focus on the pro-forma ownership split.
real-estate-investment-trusts-reits-9: Because these deals are mostly stock, so what matters is what each side contributes to the combined entity versus what it receives in ownership. Contribution analysis shows exactly that; value creation analysis tests whether the buyer's NAV per share rises.
real-estate-investment-trusts-reits-10: REIT LBOs rely on continual dividend recaps and debt-funded add-on acquisitions rather than pure debt paydown, and the entity must keep distributing 90% to keep its tax status — so cash keeps leaving the business.
renewables-1: Solar, wind, biofuels, storage, EVs, and diversified portfolios. Contracted assets under PPAs are valued like infrastructure on levered DCF and TEV/MW; equipment and EV makers are valued like normal industrials or growth companies.
renewables-2: TEV/MW of capacity, which separates asset base from current utilization, plus TEV/EBITDA and a levered DCF at the project level. Capacity is comparable across companies in a way that a single year's EBITDA is not.
renewables-3: Differences the megawatt count hides: longer contracted PPA terms and better counterparties, a stronger development pipeline, better resource quality and capacity factors, cheaper financing, or a friendlier regulatory regime.
renewables-4: Solar is the cheapest and most modular with predictable output. Onshore wind is larger and more variable. Offshore wind is the biggest, most capital-intensive, and hardest to build, so it needs the highest returns and the strongest contracts.
renewables-5: Producers look like chemicals companies — realized price less feedstock and processing cost, with margins that swing on the spread. Value hinges on the durability of policy credits, which can be a majority of the economics.
technology-media-telecommunications-tmt-: Technology, media, and telecom, with software, internet, hardware, semis, and IT services inside tech. Software is valued on revenue and ARR multiples, hardware and semis on EBITDA with heavy CapEx, telecom on EV/EBITDA with high leverage.

Telecom and semis are capital-intensive with high CapEx and heavy fixed assets; software is labor-intensive and asset-light. That means telecom trades on EBITDA with real leverage, while software trades on revenue growth and gross margin.
